summary: This mishnah asks when we may start saying Shema at night, and until when. The Rabbis also teach that they set an early deadline to keep people from missing the mitzvah.
stIntro: The beginning of tractate Berakhot, the first tractate in the first of the six orders of Mishna, opens with a discussion of the recitation of Shema, as the recitation of Shema encompasses an acceptance of the yoke of Heaven and of the mitzvot, and as such, forms the basis for all subsequent teachings. The Mishna opens with the laws regarding the appropriate time to recite Shema:

chunks.en: From what time do we say Shema at night?
chunks.st: From when, that is, from what time, does one recite Shema in the evening?

chunks.en: From the time the Kohanim go in to eat their terumah,
chunks.st: From the time when the priests enter to partake of their teruma.

words.note: Kohanim are the family of Aharon who served in the Beis HaMikdash.
Terumah is a special gift of food given to Kohanim; they may eat it only when they are pure, after nightfall.

chunks.en: until the end of the first watch of the night.
chunks.st: Until when does the time for the recitation of the evening Shema extend? Until the end of the first watch.
chunks.stMore: The term used in the Torah (Deuteronomy 6:7) to indicate the time for the recitation of the evening Shema is beshokhbekha, when you lie down, which refers to the time in which individuals go to sleep. Therefore, the time for the recitation of Shema is the first portion of the night, when individuals typically prepare for sleep.

words.note: The night was split into three watches, like shifts of guards.

chunks.en: That is what Rabbi Eliezer says.
chunks.st: That is the statement of Rabbi Eliezer.

words.note: A great Rabbi of the Mishnah.

chunks.en: But the Sages say,
chunks.st: The Rabbis say:

chunks.en: until midnight.
chunks.st: The time for the recitation of the evening Shema is until midnight.

chunks.en: Rabban Gamliel says,
chunks.st: Rabban Gamliel says:

words.note: A title for the leader of the Jewish people.
A great Rabbi of the Mishnah, head of the Sanhedrin.

chunks.en: until dawn.
chunks.st: One may recite Shema until dawn,
chunks.stMore: indicating that beshokhbekha is to be understood as a reference to the entire time people sleep in their beds, the whole night. The mishna relates that Rabban Gamliel practiced in accordance with his ruling.

words.note: The first light that shows in the sky before sunrise.

chunks.en: Once his sons came home late from a wedding party.
chunks.st: There was an incident where Rabban Gamliel’s sons returned very late from a wedding hall.

chunks.en: They said to him,
chunks.st: They said to him,
chunks.stMore: as they had been preoccupied with celebrating with the groom and bride:

chunks.en: "We did not say Shema yet."
chunks.st: We did not recite Shema.

chunks.en: He said to them,
chunks.st: He said to them:

chunks.en: "If dawn has not come up yet,
chunks.st: If the dawn has not yet arrived,

chunks.en: you still must say it.
chunks.st: you are obligated to recite Shema.
chunks.stMore: Since Rabban Gamliel’s opinion disagreed with that of the Rabbis, he explained to his sons that the Rabbis actually agree with him,

chunks.en: And not only this,
chunks.st: and that it is not only with regard to the halakha of the recitation of Shema,

chunks.en: but everything that the Sages said
chunks.st: but rather, wherever the Sages say

chunks.en: should be done by midnight,
chunks.st: until midnight,

chunks.en: may really be done until dawn.
chunks.st: the mitzva may be performed until dawn.

chunks.en: Burning the fats and limbs of korbanos on the mizbeach
chunks.st: Rabban Gamliel cites several cases in support of his claim, such as the burning of fats and limbs on the altar.

words.note: Special fat parts of a korban that were burned on the mizbeach.
Parts of a korban burned whole on the mizbeach.

chunks.en: may be done until dawn.
chunks.st: Due to the quantity of offerings each day, the priests were often unable to complete the burning of all of the fats and limbs, so they continued to be burned into the night,
chunks.stMore: as it is written: “This is the law of the burnt offering: The burnt offering shall remain upon the pyre on the altar all night until morning, while the fire on the altar burns it” (Leviticus 6:2).

chunks.en: And all korbanos that are eaten for one day and night
chunks.st: And, with regard to all sacrifices, such as the sin-offerings and the guilt-offerings that are eaten for one day and night;

chunks.en: may be eaten until dawn.
chunks.st: although the Sages state that they may be eaten only until midnight, by Torah law they may be eaten until dawn.
chunks.stMore: This is in accordance with the verse: “On the day on which it is offered must you eat. Do not leave it until the morning” (Leviticus 7:15).

chunks.en: If so,
chunks.st: If so,

chunks.en: why did the Sages say "until midnight"?
chunks.st: why did the Sages say that they may be eaten only until midnight?

chunks.he: כְּדֵי לְהַרְחִיק אֶת הָאָדָם מִן הָעֲבֵרָה:
chunks.en: To keep a person far away from sinning.
chunks.st: This is in order to distance a person from transgression,
chunks.stMore: as if one believes that he has until dawn to perform the mitzva, he might be negligent and postpone it until the opportunity to perform the mitzva has passed.

summary: This mishnah teaches when we may start saying Shema in the morning, and until when.

chunks.en: From what time do we say Shema in the morning?
chunks.st: From when does one recite Shema in the morning?

chunks.en: From when one can tell techeiles blue from white.
chunks.st: From when a person can distinguish between sky-blue [tekhelet] and white.

words.note: Techeiles is the special blue color used in tzitzis.

chunks.en: Rabbi Eliezer says,
chunks.st: Rabbi Eliezer says:

words.note: A great Rabbi of the Mishnah.

chunks.en: From when one can tell techeiles blue from leek-green.
chunks.st: From when one can distinguish between sky-blue and leek-green.

words.note: A leek is a green vegetable whose color is close to blue.

chunks.en: And one must finish it by sunrise.
chunks.st: And one must finish reciting Shema until the end of the period when you rise, i.e., sunrise, when the sun begins to shine.

chunks.en: Rabbi Yehoshua says,
chunks.st: Rabbi Yehoshua says:

words.note: A great Rabbi of the Mishnah.

chunks.en: until three hours into the day,
chunks.st: One may recite the morning Shema until three hours of the day, which this is still considered when you rise,

chunks.en: because that is the way of kings and princes:
chunks.st: as that is the habit of kings to rise from their sleep
chunks.basisNote: Steinsaltz says kings; Bartenura says the sons of kings.

chunks.en: to get up three hours into the day.
chunks.st: at three hours of the day.

chunks.en: Someone who says it later did not lose anything;
chunks.st: While there is a set time frame for the recitation of Shema, one who recites Shema from that time onward loses nothing.
chunks.stMore: Although he does not fulfill the mitzva of reciting of Shema at its appointed time,
chunks.basisNote: Bartenura adds: he still says the brachos of Shema.

chunks.en: he is like a person reading from the Torah, and he gets reward for that.
chunks.st: he is nevertheless considered like one who reads the Torah, and is rewarded accordingly.

summary: Beis Shammai and Beis Hillel argue about whether we must lie down at night and stand in the morning to say Shema. The halacha follows Beis Hillel: say it however you are.
stIntro: Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel disputed the proper way to recite Shema.

chunks.en: Beis Shammai say,
chunks.st: Beit Shammai say:
chunks.stMore: One should recite Shema in the manner indicated in the text of Shema itself. Therefore,

words.note: Beis Shammai were the students of Shammai, a great early Sage.

chunks.en: at night everyone must lie down on his side and say Shema,
chunks.st: in the evening every person must recline on his side and recite Shema,
chunks.stMore: in fulfillment of the verse: “When you lie down,”

chunks.en: and in the morning he must stand,
chunks.st: and in the morning he must stand and recite Shema,
chunks.stMore: in fulfillment of the verse: When you rise,

chunks.en: as it says, "when you lie down and when you get up."
chunks.st: as it is stated: “When you lie down, and when you rise.”

chunks.en: And Beis Hillel say,
chunks.st: And Beit Hillel say:

words.note: Beis Hillel were the students of Hillel, a great early Sage.

chunks.en: everyone says it in whatever way he is,
chunks.explain: Standing, sitting, lying down, or walking.
chunks.st: Every person recites Shema as he is,
chunks.stMore: and he may do so in whatever position is most comfortable for him, both day and night,

chunks.en: as it says, "and when you walk on the road."
chunks.st: as it is stated: “And when you walk along the way,” when one is neither standing nor reclining (Me’iri).

chunks.en: If so,
chunks.st: If so, according to Beit Hillel,

chunks.en: why does it say "when you lie down and when you get up"?
chunks.st: why was it stated: “When you lie down, and when you rise”?

chunks.en: It means at the time people go to sleep,
chunks.st: This is merely to denote time; at the time when people lie down

chunks.en: and at the time people get up.
chunks.st: and the time when people rise.

chunks.en: Rabbi Tarfon said,
chunks.st: With regard to this halakha, Rabbi Tarfon said:

words.note: A great Rabbi of the Mishnah.

chunks.en: "I was traveling on the road,
chunks.st: Once, I was coming on the road

chunks.en: and I lay down on my side to say Shema,
chunks.st: when I stopped and reclined to recite Shema

words.en: and I lay on my side

chunks.en: like Beis Shammai say,
chunks.st: in accordance with the statement of Beit Shammai.
chunks.stMore: Although Rabbi Tarfon was a disciple of Beit Hillel, he thought that fulfilling the mitzva in accordance with the opinion of Beit Shammai would be a more meticulous fulfillment of the mitzva, acceptable to all opinions.

chunks.en: and I put myself in danger from robbers."
chunks.st: Yet in so doing, I endangered myself due to the highwaymen [listim] who accost travelers.

chunks.en: They said to him,
chunks.st: The Sages said to him:

chunks.en: "You deserved to pay with your life,
chunks.st: You deserved to be in a position where you were liable to pay with your life,

chunks.en: because you went against Beis Hillel."
chunks.st: as you transgressed the statement of Beit Hillel.
chunks.stMore: This statement will be explained in the Gemara.

summary: This mishnah tells how many brachos we say before and after Shema, and that we must not change the way the Sages wrote each bracha.
stIntro: From the laws of the recitation of Shema itself, the mishna proceeds to discuss the blessings recited in conjunction with Shema. Here, the order is established:

chunks.he: בַּשַּׁחַר מְבָרֵךְ שְׁתַּיִם לְפָנֶיהָ וְאַחַת לְאַחֲרֶיהָ,
chunks.en: In the morning one says two brachos before it and one after it,
chunks.st: In the morning when reciting Shema, one recites two blessings beforehand, the first on the radiant lights and the second the blessing on the love of Torah, and one thereafter, which begins with: True and Firm [emet veyatziv].

chunks.en: and at night two before it and two after it.
chunks.st: And in the evening one recites two blessings beforehand, on the radiant lights and on the love of God, and two thereafter, the blessing of redemption: True and Faithful [emet ve’emuna], and the blessing: Help us lie down.

chunks.en: One is long and one is short.
chunks.explain: A long bracha starts and ends with Baruch; a short one only ends with it.
chunks.st: With regard to the blessing: True and Faithful, whether one recites it in its long formula and whether one recites it in its short formula, he fulfills his obligation (Tosafot).
chunks.basisNote: Steinsaltz reads it as: Emes VeEmunah may be said long or short. Bartenura fits our words.

chunks.en: Where the Sages said to make it long,
chunks.st: However, the general principle is: Where the Sages said to recite a long blessing,

chunks.en: one may not make it short.
chunks.st: one may not shorten it,

chunks.en: Where they said to make it short, one may not make it long.
chunks.st: and so too, wherever they said to recite a short blessing, one may not lengthen it.

chunks.en: Where they said to end with "Baruch," one may not skip it.
chunks.st: Where the Sages said that a blessing must conclude with a second blessing at the end, he may not fail to conclude with that blessing.

words.note: Closing a bracha means ending it with "Baruch Atah Hashem..."

chunks.en: And where they said not to end that way,
chunks.st: Similarly, if the Sages said that a blessing must not conclude with a second blessing,

chunks.en: one may not add an ending.
chunks.st: one may not conclude with a blessing.

summary: We remember leaving Egypt every night too, in the last part of Shema. Ben Zoma learned this from a pasuk, and the Sages learned that we will remember it even in the days of Mashiach.
stIntro: It is a mitzva by Torah law to mention the exodus from Egypt at night, but some held that this mitzva was, like phylacteries or ritual fringes, fulfilled only during the day and not at night. For this reason it was decided:

chunks.en: We mention leaving Egypt at night.
chunks.st: The exodus from Egypt is mentioned at night, adjacent to the recitation of Shema.

chunks.en: Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah said,
chunks.st: Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya said:

words.note: A great Rabbi of the Mishnah who became head of the Sanhedrin when he was very young.

chunks.en: "I am about seventy years old,
chunks.st: I am approximately seventy years old, and

chunks.he: וְלֹא זָכִיתִי שֶׁתֵּאָמֵר יְצִיאַת מִצְרַיִם בַּלֵּילוֹת,
chunks.en: and I could not prove that leaving Egypt must be said at night,
chunks.st: although I have long held this opinion, I was never privileged to prevail (Me’iri) and prove that there is a biblical obligation to fulfill the accepted custom (Ra’avad) and have the exodus from Egypt mentioned at night,

chunks.en: until Ben Zoma explained it,
chunks.st: until Ben Zoma interpreted it homiletically and proved it obligatory.

words.note: A great Rabbi of the Mishnah, famous for explaining pesukim.

chunks.en: as it says, "So that you will remember
chunks.st: Ben Zoma derived it as it is stated: “That you may remember

chunks.en: the day you left the land of Egypt
chunks.st: the day you went out of the land of Egypt

chunks.en: all the days of your life."
chunks.st: all the days of your life” (Deuteronomy 16:3).

chunks.en: "The days of your life" means
chunks.st: The days of your life,

chunks.en: the days. "All the days of your life"
chunks.st: refers to daytime alone; however, the addition of the word all, as it is stated: All the days of your life,

chunks.en: adds the nights. But the Sages say,
chunks.st: comes to add nights as well. And the Rabbis,
chunks.stMore: who posit that there is no biblical obligation to mention the exodus from Egypt at night, explain the word, all, differently and say:

chunks.en: "The days of your life" means
chunks.st: The days of your life, refers to the days in

chunks.en: this world.
chunks.st: this world,

chunks.en: "All the days of your life"
chunks.st: all is added

chunks.en: adds the days of Mashiach.
chunks.st: to include the days of the Messiah.
